preamble: Backing and rounding of [i] to [u] is rare as a regular change but occurs as a conditioned assimilation after labials, especially the rounded labial-velar glide [w], which spreads its rounding and backness to the following high vowel. In Old English, early widu 'wood' and widuwe 'widow' developed variants wudu and wuduwe; wudu became the standard form and survives as Modern English wood. The same rounding after w recurred in Middle English, where wimman 'woman' became wumman, womman [ˈwuman] from the 13th century in western England, the source of the modern singular /ˈwʊmən/.

examples.note: Assimilated after w; wudu is the usual later form and the ancestor of Modern English wood.
West Saxon variant with the same rounding after w.

Rounding under the influence of the preceding w, first in western England in the 13th century; the unrounded form survived into the 15th century and in the plural, giving Modern English woman /ˈwʊmən/ beside women /ˈwɪmɪn/.
